title: Cross-SDK fetch shim for paged vector + reranker workflows: checkpointed streaming, graceful retries, and ergonomic examples
creator: Morgan Li
description: Problem statement: SDK users (Python/TS/Go) implementing multi-stage vector workflows (paged embedding generation followed by batched reranking) face glue-code complexity: resumable pagination, transient network errors during streaming, ordering guarantees for reranking, and inconsistent ergonomics across SDKs. Goal: deliver a small cross-language "fetch shim" pattern and library helpers that make paged vector + reranker flows easy to implement with safe defaults for batching, checkpointed streaming, exponential backoff with jitter, cancellation tokens, and deterministic rerank ordering.
acceptance_criteria: 1) Libraries / example helpers in Python, TypeScript, and Go that demonstrate: a) fetching embeddings in pages with cursor checkpointing b) streaming tokens/results with cancel/timeout support c) automatic best-effort resume from last checkpoint on transient failures d) deterministic ordering when feeding batched reranker requests e) sensible defaults for batch sizes/timeout/backoff with overrides. 2) Unit + integration tests that simulate network failures, retries, and ordering. 3) Docs + three runnable examples (one per language) added to SDK examples repo. 4) API reviewed and approved by SDK leads (PM + eng).
design_notes:
- Provide a tiny language-idiomatic adapter per SDK (iterator/generator in Python, AsyncIterable + helper in TS, channel-like iterator in Go).
- Checkpoint model: persist last-successful-page-cursor (string) and last-output-index for reranker ordering. Avoid heavy durable storage; examples will show saving to local file/kv.
- Retry policy: exponential backoff with full jitter by default, max attempts = 5, retry on idempotent fetch errors and stream interruptions; do NOT retry non-idempotent commit operations.
- Streaming ergonomics: expose non-blocking cancel token and per-item acknowledgement so caller can checkpoint mid-stream.
- Reranker ordering: canonical approach: preserve original embedding index in metadata and group-sort server-side where available, otherwise sort client-side before calling reranker batch. Examples will include stable-key metadata.
- Backpressure: adapt fetch rate if reranker backlog grows beyond threshold; provide a simple bounded queue example in each language.
- Backwards compatibility: keep helpers additive and opt-in; original low-level SDK APIs unchanged.
tradeoffs:
- We avoid introducing a persistent queue service; that keeps SDKs lightweight but shifts durability responsibility to the integrator for very large workloads.
- Choosing default batch sizes (128 embeddings / 32 reranker items) is a heuristic: smaller defaults reduce latency but increase RPC count. We'll expose defaults and making them configurable.
- Client-side ordering vs server feature: prefer server-side stable sorting when available; fallback to client sorting which increases memory footprint for large batches.
implementation_plan: 1) Spec and API surface (this ticket) — sketches for each SDK (2d) 2) Python adapter (3d): generator + checkpoint helper + example notebook 3) TypeScript adapter (4d): AsyncIterable + AbortSignal + example repo integration 4) Go adapter (4d): channel-based stream + context cancellation + example CLI 5) Tests + chaos injection harness (2d) 6) Docs, examples PRs, and SDK leads review (2d) 7) Merge and announce (1d)
testing_strategy:
- Unit tests for backoff math, cursor persistence, and ordering.
- Integration tests that spin up a test harness mocking embedding + rerank endpoints to inject latency/errors.
- Fuzz: random failures mid-stream and verify resume correctness.
- Performance smoke: end-to-end with 10k items to validate memory/batching heuristics.
